title: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway story
meta_description: How a 2 ft gauge tramway climbed from the plains to Ghum in 1881, why UNESCO listed it in 1999, and where to see its loops, reverses and steam engines today.
summary: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway climbs about 88 km from New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling on 2 ft (610 mm) track, topping out at Ghum, 2,258 m. It opened to Darjeeling on 4 July 1881, uses loops and Z-reverses instead of tunnels, and in 1999 became the first railway in Asia on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

sections.heading: Why a railway was needed
paras: By the 1870s Darjeeling was a busy sanatorium and the centre of a tea industry that had grown from Archibald Campbell's first seeds in 1841 to dozens of gardens. Everything moved up and down the hill by bullock cart, pony and porter along the Hill Cart Road. Rice, coal and machinery went up; tea chests came down. The journey from the plains took days, and freight costs ate into the planters' profits.

In 1878 Franklin Prestage, an agent of the Eastern Bengal Railway, proposed a steam tramway along the existing cart road from Siliguri to Darjeeling. The Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, Sir Ashley Eden, backed the idea, and a committee found it workable. The Darjeeling Steam Tramway Company was formed, with the Calcutta firm of Gillanders, Arbuthnot and Company as agents, and work began in 1879.

The cart road itself was a big step. Before it, the way up was a bridle path through malarial forest at the foot of the hills, and many early visitors arrived exhausted or ill. The road made wheeled traffic possible, but a loaded cart still needed several days to climb, and the bullocks that pulled it died in large numbers. A railway on the same alignment promised to do the trip in hours, at a fraction of the cost per ton.

sections.heading: Building the line, 1879–1881
paras: The builders chose a gauge of just 2 ft (610 mm), which allowed tight curves on a narrow mountain road, and they kept to the cart road wherever possible to save money. The line reached Tindharia and then Kurseong in 1880, and the first train ran right through to Darjeeling on 4 July 1881. The company renamed itself the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway Company that same year.

The climb was the hard part. From about 115 m at the foot of the hills, the track has to rise to 2,258 m at Ghum. The engineers solved it without tunnels or rack rails. Where the slope was too steep, they built loops, in which the track spirals round and crosses over itself to gain height, and reverses, Z-shaped zigzags in which the train runs forward up one spur, stops, then runs backwards up the next. The loop at Agony Point, near Tindharia, is one of the tightest curves on any railway in India.

Over the years the line was realigned after landslides and to ease grades. The most famous later change is Batasia Loop, below Ghum, completed in 1919, which replaced a steep section on the descent to Darjeeling. Today the Gorkha War Memorial stands in a garden at its centre, and on a clear day Kangchenjunga rises behind it.

sections.heading: Engines, branch lines and hard years
paras: The line's best-known engines are the B class, small 0-4-0 saddle-tank steam locomotives built mostly in Glasgow between 1889 and 1925. A handful are still in service, overhauled at the railway's workshop at Tindharia, and they pull the steam joyrides from Darjeeling. Each carries a crew who sit on the front buffer beam with a box of sand, throwing it on the rails when the wheels slip on wet track.

The company also built branch lines in the plains and towards Kalimpong. The Teesta Valley line ran up the Teesta from Siliguri to Gielle Khola, below Kalimpong, from 1915; the floods of 1950 destroyed much of it, and it was never rebuilt. After independence the government bought the company in 1948, and the line became part of Indian Railways, today run by the Northeast Frontier Railway.

The main line has had hard years since. Monsoon landslides cut it often; a slip at Paglajhora in 2010 closed the lower section for several years. Political agitation for Gorkhaland has also halted services, and stations were damaged in 2017. Each time, the railway has come back, slowly, because the hills, the town and the tourism industry want it running.

sections.heading: Why UNESCO listed it
paras: In December 1999 UNESCO inscribed the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway on the World Heritage list. It was the first railway in Asia to be listed, and only the second in the world after Austria's Semmering Railway. UNESCO cited it as an outstanding example of a bold, ingenious engineering solution for establishing an effective rail link across a mountainous terrain of great beauty, and as a line still in working use much as it was built.

The listing was extended in 2005 to include the Nilgiri Mountain Railway in Tamil Nadu, and in 2008 the Kalka–Shimla Railway, under the joint name Mountain Railways of India. The Darjeeling line is the oldest of the three. The listing brings duties too: the railway has to protect the old stations, the track layout and the steam engines, which is why heritage steam still runs on a line where diesel would be cheaper.

sections.heading: The train in films and memory
paras: For many Indian families the train is familiar before they ever see it. In the 1969 Hindi film Aradhana, Rajesh Khanna sings Mere Sapno Ki Rani from an open jeep racing beside the toy train on the Hill Cart Road, and that scene sent generations of honeymooners to Darjeeling. The line has appeared in many films since, including the 2012 Hindi film Barfi, shot partly around Darjeeling.

Local memory is different. Older residents of Kurseong and Sonada remember the train as a lifeline: the way children went to school, how vegetables reached market, and the sound that told you the time of day. Shopkeepers in Kurseong bazaar still pull their goods back from the rails when they hear the whistle.

sections.heading: How to see the line today
paras: The easiest way is the joyride from Darjeeling to Ghum and back, about two hours, with a stop of about 10 minutes at Batasia Loop and about 30 minutes at the Ghum museum. Steam seats cost about ₹1,500–1,600 and diesel ₹800–1,000, indicative 2026, booked on IRCTC. A through train between NJP and Darjeeling, taking seven to eight hours, has run in recent years when the track allows, and there are passenger services between Kurseong and Darjeeling. Timetables change with repairs and the monsoon, so check current status before you travel.

You can also see a lot for free. Stand at the roadside in Kurseong bazaar, in Ghum or at Batasia Loop when a train is due, or follow the Hill Cart Road down from Kurseong to see the loops and reverses at Tindharia, Gayabari and Rangtong. In late November and early December, the Ghum Festival of the DHR brings special runs, exhibitions and events at the stations.
list: Book joyrides and passenger trains on IRCTC as soon as your dates are fixed; October, May and June sell out.
Sit on the valley side going up from Darjeeling to Ghum for the best view at Batasia Loop.
Carry a jacket: the coaches are not heated, and Ghum is often foggy and cold.
Keep well back from the rails in Kurseong and Ghum bazaars; the train runs on the road itself.
If the train is suspended, visit the Ghum museum by road and watch the steam engines being prepared in Darjeeling yard in the morning.

faqs.q: When was the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway built
faqs.a: Construction began in 1879, after Franklin Prestage of the Eastern Bengal Railway proposed a steam tramway along the Hill Cart Road in 1878. The line reached Kurseong in 1880, and the first train ran through to Darjeeling on 4 July 1881. The company took the name Darjeeling Himalayan Railway Company that year.

faqs.q: Why is it called the toy train
faqs.a: Because everything about it is small. The track is just 2 ft (610 mm) between the rails, the B-class steam engines are tiny 0-4-0 saddle tanks, and the coaches are narrow, with seats for only a few people across. Visitors began calling it the toy train long ago, and the name is now used officially in tourism material.

faqs.q: How long is the Darjeeling toy train route
faqs.a: About 88 km from New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling, climbing from roughly 115 m to 2,258 m at Ghum before dropping slightly to Darjeeling at about 2,075 m. The full run takes seven to eight hours when the through train operates. The popular joyride covers only the 7 km between Darjeeling and Ghum.

faqs.q: What are the loops and reverses on the DHR
faqs.a: They are how the train climbs without tunnels. A loop is a spiral where the track turns a full circle and crosses over itself to gain height, as at Agony Point and Batasia. A reverse is a Z-shaped zigzag: the train runs up one arm, stops, and runs backwards up the next, gaining height at each turn.

faqs.q: Is the Darjeeling railway a UNESCO World Heritage Site
faqs.a: Yes. UNESCO inscribed it in December 1999, the first railway in Asia and the second in the world after Austria's Semmering line. In 2005 and 2008 the listing was extended to the Nilgiri and Kalka–Shimla railways under the name Mountain Railways of India. Darjeeling's is the oldest of the three.

Several are. The B-class engines still working on the line were built mostly in Glasgow between 1889 and 1925 and have been rebuilt and overhauled many times at the Tindharia workshop. Some have been converted to burn oil instead of coal. Diesel engines now handle most regular services, while steam pulls the heritage joyrides.

faqs.q: Which film made the Darjeeling toy train famous
faqs.a: Aradhana, released in 1969. In the song Mere Sapno Ki Rani, Rajesh Khanna sings from an open jeep beside the toy train while Sharmila Tagore watches from the coach window. The scene is one of the best-known in Hindi cinema and made the train a symbol of Darjeeling holidays.

faqs.q: What was the Teesta Valley line
faqs.a: A branch of the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway that ran from Siliguri up the Teesta valley to Gielle Khola, below Kalimpong, from 1915. It carried passengers and freight, including goods for the Tibet trade through Kalimpong. Floods in 1950 destroyed large parts of it, and it was never rebuilt. Traces of the alignment remain along the river.

faqs.q: Does the full NJP to Darjeeling train run every day
faqs.a: Not always. The through train has run daily in some seasons and been suspended in others because of landslides, track work and the monsoon. Joyrides from Darjeeling and Kurseong–Darjeeling services run more regularly. Look on IRCTC for your dates, and check current status before you travel.
